stem: Which HTTP method does Next.js use when the client invokes a Server Action?

options.text: `POST`, and only `POST` can invoke an action
options.why: Actions are dispatched as POST requests to the page; other methods cannot trigger them.

options.text: `GET`, so the result can be cached by the browser
options.why: A mutation over GET would be cacheable and prefetchable, which is exactly what actions avoid.

options.text: `PUT` for updates and `DELETE` for deletions
options.why: Next.js does not map actions to REST verbs; every action uses the same method.

options.text: Whatever method the `<form method>` attribute says
options.why: The form's `method` attribute does not change how React dispatches a function action.

explanation: Behind the scenes, Server Actions use the `POST` method, and only this HTTP method can invoke them. That also means an action is reachable by anyone who can send the same POST, so it must authenticate and authorize itself.
reference: Next.js docs: Mutating Data

stem: In Next.js you can define a Server Function inline inside a Client Component by putting `'use server'` at the top of the function body.

options.text: True
options.why: Inline `'use server'` functions are only supported inside Server Components.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Client Components cannot define Server Functions; they import them from a `'use server'` file or receive them as props.

explanation: The Next.js docs state that it is not possible to define Server Functions in Client Components. Put them in a separate file that starts with `'use server'` and import them, or define them inline in a Server Component and pass them down as a prop.
reference: Next.js docs: Mutating Data (Client Components)

stem: With no extra configuration, what is the maximum request body size Next.js accepts for a Server Action?

options.text: 100 KB
options.why: That is lower than the real default; small form posts would rarely hit it either way.

options.text: 1 MB
options.why: The default `serverActions.bodySizeLimit` is 1MB.

options.text: 4.5 MB
options.why: That number is a hosting platform limit for function payloads, not the Next.js action default.

options.text: Unlimited until the server runs out of memory
options.why: Next.js caps action bodies to protect against resource exhaustion.

explanation: Action requests are capped at 1MB by default to prevent excessive parsing work and denial of service. Raise it with `experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit` (for example `'3mb'`) when you accept larger uploads.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions config (bodySizeLimit)

stem: Type the name of the function you import from `next/cache` inside a Server Action to refetch the current route's RSC payload without invalidating any cached data.
explanation: `refresh()` refreshes the client router from within a Server Action, so the UI reflects state the action changed outside the cache. It does not revalidate tagged data; use `updateTag` or `revalidateTag` for that.
reference: Next.js docs: refresh

stem: A form action does `const data = Object.fromEntries(formData)` and logs the result. Besides the form's own fields, what else can appear in the object?

options.text: Extra properties whose names start with `$ACTION_`
options.why: The docs warn these framework fields are included in the FormData.

options.text: The user's cookies, copied in by Next.js
options.why: Cookies travel in headers; read them with `cookies()`, not from FormData.

options.text: A `__session` key holding the decoded auth token
options.why: Next.js never puts session data into the submitted FormData.

options.text: Nothing else: FormData only ever contains named inputs
options.why: Next.js adds its own `$ACTION_`-prefixed fields to action submissions.

explanation: When you collapse FormData with `Object.fromEntries()`, the object contains extra properties prefixed with `$ACTION_`. Pick the fields you need explicitly, or parse with a schema that strips unknown keys, before passing data on.
reference: Next.js docs: Forms guide

stem: A Client Component needs to call a Server Action. Which approach does Next.js support?

options.text: Define the action inline in the Client Component with `'use server'`
options.why: Inline Server Functions are not allowed in Client Components.

options.text: Import it from a `'use server'` file, or receive it as a prop
options.why: Both are documented ways to hand an action to client code.

options.text: Call `fetch('/api/actions/name')`, which Next.js creates for each action
options.why: Actions get encrypted IDs, not readable `/api` routes.

options.text: Wrap the Client Component in `<ServerAction>` from `next/server`
options.why: There is no such component; actions are plain imported functions.

explanation: Server Functions can be imported into Client Components from a dedicated `'use server'` file, or created in a Server Component and passed down as a prop such as `updateItemAction`. The compiler swaps the implementation for a reference that POSTs back to the server.
reference: Next.js docs: Mutating Data (Client Components, Passing actions as props)

stem: Which elements can invoke a Server Action directly through an `action` or `formAction` prop, without an event handler? (Choose three.)

options.text: `<form action={save}>`
options.why: React extends `<form>` so its `action` prop accepts a function.

options.text: `<button formAction={save}>` inside a form
options.why: A submit button can override the form's action with `formAction`.

options.text: `<input type="submit" formAction={save}>` inside a form
options.why: Submit inputs, like submit buttons, accept `formAction`.

options.text: `<a href={save}>`
options.why: Links navigate; they do not accept functions as a submission target.

options.text: `<div action={save}>`
options.why: `action` has no meaning on a div, so nothing is submitted.

explanation: Server Actions are invoked through `<form action>` or through `formAction` on elements nested in a form: `<button>`, `<input type="submit">` and `<input type="image">`. Anything else needs an event handler or `useEffect`, ideally wrapped in `startTransition`.
reference: Next.js docs: Forms guide (Nested form elements)

stem: A Server Component page tries to log a user out with `(await cookies()).delete('session')` during render when `?logout=1` is present. What happens?

options.text: The cookie is deleted and the page renders as logged out
options.why: Rendering cannot write cookies, because the response headers may already be streaming.

options.text: It is not allowed; set cookies in a Server Function instead
options.why: Next.js prevents setting or deleting cookies while a Server Component renders.

options.text: The cookie is deleted only on the next request
options.why: There is no deferred write; the operation simply is not allowed in render.

options.text: It works, but only in development mode
options.why: The restriction applies to every environment.

explanation: Setting or deleting cookies is not supported during Server Component rendering, because HTTP does not allow setting cookies after streaming starts. Mutations should never be a side effect of rendering. Use a Server Action, for example a logout form, or a Route Handler.
reference: Next.js docs: cookies; Data Security (avoiding side-effects during rendering)

stem: Match each call inside a Server Action with what it does.

options.text: Expires the tag at once; the action's own re-render waits for fresh data
Marks the tag stale; readers get stale data while it refreshes in the background
Invalidates cached data for one URL path
Refetches the current route without invalidating any cache

explanation: `updateTag` gives read-your-own-writes and is only allowed in Server Actions. `revalidateTag` with the `max` profile is stale-while-revalidate, so the response that comes back with the action does not wait for new data. `revalidatePath` works by URL, and `refresh` only refetches the route's RSC payload.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations (Choosing a cache update)

stem: A Server Component renders a form whose Server Action calls `redirect('/orders')`. A user submits it before any JavaScript has loaded, so the browser does a native form POST. Type the HTTP status code of the redirect response Next.js sends.
explanation: In a Server Action, `redirect` performs a client-side navigation when JavaScript is available. For progressive-enhancement form submissions it serves a `303 See Other`, so the browser follows up with a GET. Elsewhere `redirect` uses 307.
reference: Next.js docs: redirect

stem: After a Server Action calls `redirect('/posts/42')`, the user presses the browser Back button. Where do they land, and why?

options.text: Back on the form page: actions redirect with `push`
options.why: Actions add a history entry; elsewhere the default is `replace`.

options.text: Two pages back, because `redirect` always replaces history
options.why: `replace` is the default outside Server Actions, not inside them.

options.text: On `/posts/42` again, because redirects disable the Back button
options.why: Redirects never block history navigation.

options.text: On a blank page, because the POST has to be resubmitted
options.why: With JavaScript the action navigates client-side, so there is no POST to resubmit.

explanation: `redirect(path, type)` uses `push` by default in Server Actions and `replace` everywhere else. With push, the form page stays in history, so Back returns to it. Pass `RedirectType.replace` if you want the form to disappear from history.
reference: Next.js docs: redirect (type parameter)

stem: A Client Component passes a `userId` to a Server Action either with `updateUser.bind(null, userId)` or with `<input type="hidden" name="userId" value={userId} />`. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The hidden input's value is part of the rendered HTML and is not encoded
options.why: The docs call this out as the main difference from `bind`.

options.text: Either way the value arrives in a POST the caller can forge, so the action must authorize it
options.why: Anything the client sends, bound or not, is untrusted input.

options.text: Values passed with `bind` are verified by Next.js, so authorization can be skipped
options.why: Next.js does not check that a bound value belongs to the caller.

options.text: `bind` only works in Server Components, so a Client Component must use the hidden input
options.why: `bind` works in both Server and Client Components.

options.text: Only the hidden-input version works before JavaScript loads
options.why: `bind` also supports progressive enhancement.

explanation: `bind` lets you pass extra arguments ahead of the FormData and works in both component types, with progressive enhancement. A hidden input exposes its value in the HTML. Neither is a security boundary: the action should derive identity from the session and check that the user may act on that ID.
reference: Next.js docs: Forms guide (Passing additional arguments); Server Actions (Security)

stem: A CMS webhook hits `app/api/cms/route.ts`, which calls `updateTag('posts')` so the next visitor sees fresh posts. What happens?

options.text: It works; `updateTag` expires the tag from any server context
options.why: `updateTag` is restricted to Server Actions.

options.text: It throws; use `revalidateTag('posts', { expire: 0 })`
options.why: That is the documented way to expire data immediately outside an action.

options.text: It silently does nothing; the next request still serves stale posts
options.why: The docs say the call throws an error rather than being ignored.

options.text: It works, but only when the route exports `dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`
options.why: Route segment config does not change where `updateTag` may run.

explanation: `updateTag` can only be called from within Server Actions; calling it in a Route Handler throws. When the invalidation comes from outside an action, such as a webhook, call `revalidateTag(tag, { expire: 0 })` for immediate expiry, or `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')` for stale-while-revalidate.
reference: Next.js docs: updateTag; revalidateTag

stem: Calling `refresh()` from `next/cache` at the end of a Server Action also revalidates data cached with `cacheTag('posts')`.

options.text: True
options.why: `refresh` only refetches the route; it leaves tagged cache entries alone.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `refresh()` does not revalidate tagged data, so cached reads can still be stale.

explanation: `refresh()` refetches the current route's RSC payload so the router reflects the latest state, but it does not revalidate tagged data. If the page reads from a `'use cache'` function tagged `posts`, call `updateTag('posts')` (or `revalidateTag`) as well.
reference: Next.js docs: Mutating Data (Refresh data)

stem: A profile form uploads a 1.5 MB avatar through a Server Action. Small images work, but this one fails before the action's code runs. What is the fix?

options.text: Send the file as base64 inside a hidden input instead
options.why: Base64 makes the body about a third larger, so the limit is hit sooner.

options.text: Add `export const maxDuration = 60` to the page
options.why: `maxDuration` limits execution time, not request body size.

options.text: Raise `serverActions.bodySizeLimit`, say to `'3mb'`
options.why: Action bodies are capped at 1MB unless you configure a higher limit.

options.text: Mark the action `async` so it can stream the upload
options.why: Every Server Function is already async; that does not change the cap.

explanation: Action requests are capped at 1MB by default. Configure `serverActions.bodySizeLimit` in `next.config.js` under `experimental`, using bytes or a string such as `'3mb'`. For very large files, uploading straight to object storage with a presigned URL avoids pushing them through the action at all.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions config (bodySizeLimit)

stem: In a Client Component, a user submits a form that calls a Server Action before the page's JavaScript has finished loading. What does Next.js do?

options.text: Drops the submission, because Client Component forms need React to be running
options.why: The docs say the submission is kept, not lost.

options.text: Falls back to a full-page native POST and reload
options.why: That fallback describes Server Component forms, not this case.

options.text: Queues the submission and prioritizes that component for hydration
options.why: Once it hydrates, the queued action runs without a page refresh.

options.text: Shows a browser error until the user retries manually
options.why: Next.js handles the early submission itself.

explanation: Server Component forms are progressively enhanced: they submit even with JavaScript disabled. In Client Components, forms that invoke Server Actions queue submissions if JavaScript isn't loaded yet and are prioritized for hydration. After hydration, submissions no longer refresh the page.
reference: Next.js docs: Mutating Data (Client Components)

stem: A Client Component calls an `incrementViews()` Server Action inside `useEffect(() => { ... }, [])`. In `next dev`, each visit adds 2 views; in production it adds 1. Why?

options.text: Next.js retries every Server Action once in development
options.why: Actions are not retried automatically in any mode.

options.text: Dev Strict Mode runs the effect, cleans up, runs it again
options.why: The double run is a dev-only check that effects are resilient.

options.text: The dev server dispatches actions in parallel, so the first call is duplicated
options.why: Actions are dispatched one at a time per client.

options.text: `useEffect` runs once on the server and once on the client
options.why: Effects never run on the server.

explanation: React Strict Mode, enabled by default in the App Router during development, runs effects mount, unmount, mount to expose missing cleanups. A mutation in an effect therefore fires twice in dev. Make such actions idempotent, for example by keying a view per session, or trigger them from a user event.
reference: Next.js docs: Mutating Data (useEffect); react.dev: StrictMode

stem: A Server Action inserts a comment into the database and returns nothing. It calls no revalidation, `refresh`, cookie or `redirect` API. The comment list on the current page, rendered by a Server Component, does not change. Why?

options.text: The response carries only the return value, so the route is not re-rendered
options.why: Without one of those calls, no new RSC payload is included.

options.text: The insert ran in a transaction that Next.js rolls back without `redirect`
options.why: Next.js does not touch your database transactions.

options.text: Server Components only re-render after a full browser reload
options.why: Actions can re-render the route in the same roundtrip when asked.

options.text: Actions that return `undefined` are discarded by the client router
options.why: The return value doesn't decide whether the action's work is kept.

explanation: An action re-renders the current route in its response only when it calls `updateTag`, `revalidatePath` or `refresh`, mutates cookies, or calls `redirect`. Otherwise it carries just its return value. Add `revalidatePath('/post/1')`, `updateTag` or `refresh()` after the insert.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations (A single response carries data and UI)

stem: A theme switcher's Server Action calls `(await cookies()).set('theme', 'dark')` and returns nothing. What does the user see?

options.text: Nothing changes until they reload, because the action returned no data
options.why: Cookie changes make Next.js re-render even without a return value.

options.text: The page and layouts re-render with the new cookie
options.why: Client state is preserved for components that re-render.

options.text: A full page reload that resets all client state
options.why: The update is applied to the current React tree, not a hard reload.

options.text: An error, because cookies can only be set in Route Handlers
options.why: Server Functions are a documented place to set cookies.

explanation: When you set or delete a cookie in a Server Action, Next.js re-renders the current page and its layouts on the server so the UI reflects the new value, all in the same roundtrip. Client state is preserved for re-rendered components, and effects re-run if their dependencies changed.
reference: Next.js docs: Mutating Data (Cookies)

stem: Users reach the app at `https://shop.example.com:8443`. Next.js runs behind a proxy that passes its own internal host instead of the public one, and every Server Action is rejected by the CSRF check. Which `allowedOrigins` entry fixes it?

options.text: `'shop.example.com'`
options.why: The Origin host includes the port, and an entry without a port doesn't match it.

options.text: `'shop.example.com:8443'`
options.why: Entries match the Origin `host`, which is hostname plus port when a port is present.

options.text: `'https://shop.example.com:8443'`
options.why: Entries are hosts, not full origins with a scheme.

options.text: `'*.example.com:*'`
options.why: A port cannot be wildcarded; it must be written out in full.

explanation: Next.js compares the host in the request's `Origin` header with `x-forwarded-host` or `host`. `allowedOrigins` entries are matched against the Origin's `host`, which includes the port when the URL carries one. Ports can't be wildcarded, so write `shop.example.com:8443`, or `*.shop.example.com:8443` for subdomains.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions config (allowedOrigins)

stem: Which of these make a Server Action's response include a freshly rendered RSC payload for the current route? (Choose three.)

options.text: Calling `updateTag('cart')`
options.why: Immediate tag expiry re-renders the route in the same response.

options.text: Calling `refresh()`
options.why: It refetches the current route's RSC payload.

options.text: Calling `(await cookies()).delete('promo')`
options.why: Mutating cookies re-renders the current page automatically.

options.text: Calling `revalidateTag('cart', 'max')`
options.why: Stale-while-revalidate skips the immediate re-render; later reads see the change.

options.text: Returning `{ ok: true }` without calling anything else
options.why: Then the response carries only the return value.

options.text: Calling `after(() => log())` from `next/server`
options.why: `after` schedules work after the response; it doesn't trigger a re-render.

explanation: A re-render is included when the action calls `updateTag`, `revalidatePath` or `refresh`, mutates cookies, or calls `redirect`, which streams the destination. `revalidateTag` with a stale-while-revalidate profile is the documented exception.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations

stem: A form in a Server Component calls a Server Action that saves an order and then calls `redirect('/orders')`. JavaScript is disabled in the user's browser. Put the steps in order.

options.text: The browser sends a native form POST to the page
Next.js runs the action, which saves the order
The action calls `redirect`, which throws a control-flow exception
Next.js responds with `303 See Other` and a `Location` of `/orders`
The browser follows the redirect with a GET to `/orders`

explanation: Server Component forms submit even without JavaScript. The action runs, and `redirect` throws so nothing after it executes. For a progressive-enhancement submission, Next.js answers with a 303, which tells the browser to fetch the destination with GET. With JavaScript, the same action would perform a client-side navigation instead.
reference: Next.js docs: redirect; Mutating Data

options.text: The whole updated row, including fields like `passwordHash`, is sent to the client
options.why: Return values are serialized to the client, so return only what the UI needs.

options.text: Any submitted field, such as `role=admin`, is written to the user record
options.why: Spreading raw FormData into an update lets the caller choose columns.

options.text: The action is unauthenticated because `auth()` cannot run in a Server Action
options.why: Actions can read cookies and sessions; `auth()` works here.

options.text: `db.user.update` cannot be awaited inside a `'use server'` file
options.why: Server Functions are ordinary async functions on the server.

options.text: Returning a value from a form action makes React submit the form twice
options.why: Return values do not cause resubmission.

explanation: Two separate leaks: input and output. `Object.fromEntries(formData)` includes every posted key, plus Next.js's `$ACTION_` fields, so validate with a schema that picks the allowed fields. Returning the raw record exposes internal columns. Return something minimal like `{ success: true }`.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Controlling return values); Forms guide

stem: Right after a deployment, some users clicking "Save" get the error "Failed to find Server Action". Users who reload the page are fine. What is the cause?

options.text: The new build disabled actions, because `serverActions` must be re-enabled after each deploy
options.why: Actions are enabled by default and stay enabled.

options.text: Their open tabs run the old client, which calls an action ID the new build no longer has
options.why: New builds typically generate new action IDs.

options.text: The CDN cached the POST response from before the deploy
options.why: Action POSTs are not served from a CDN cache.

options.text: The request body is over 1 MB after the deploy
options.why: Body size errors don't depend on deployments or reloads.

explanation: Each Server Action is identified by an ID in the build artifacts, and new deployments typically generate new IDs. They rotate at most every 14 days even when the source is unchanged. A client still running the previous build can invoke a missing ID. Prefer rolling deployments, keep `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` stable, and treat the error as a retry path in the UI.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations (Deployment considerations)

stem: You self-host one build on three instances behind a round-robin load balancer. Inline Server Actions that capture variables from their Server Component fail on some requests but not others. What should you configure?

options.text: The same base64 `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` on every instance
options.why: Closure variables are encrypted, so every instance must use the same key.

options.text: Sticky sessions so each user always reaches the instance that rendered the page
options.why: This hides the symptom and breaks again on failover; a shared key fixes the cause.

options.text: `serverActions.allowedOrigins` listing each instance's IP address
options.why: The CSRF check compares Origin with host; it has nothing to do with decryption.

options.text: A higher `serverActions.bodySizeLimit`, because closures enlarge the request
options.why: The failures are decryption mismatches, not body size.

explanation: Variables captured by an inline action are encrypted before being sent to the client. When self-hosting across multiple servers, each instance may otherwise use a different key. Set `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` to a stable, base64-encoded 16, 24 or 32-byte key (for example from `openssl rand -base64 32`) shared by every instance.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Overwriting encryption keys)

options.text: Version 1, because TypeScript guarantees `item` is a valid `Item`
options.why: Types vanish at runtime; a forged POST can send any object.

options.text: Version 2, because schema validation proves the item is legitimate
options.why: Zod checks shape only; a well-formed item can belong to someone else.

options.text: Version 3, because it takes only an ID and checks ownership via the session
options.why: Identity comes from the session and access is checked in the query.

options.text: All three, because unused actions are stripped from the client bundle
options.why: This action is used, so it has a reachable endpoint.

explanation: The docs' guidance: the client may say which item to act on, but should not supply its contents or ownership. Send an ID plus the change, then re-read the row from a trusted source filtered by the session user. Schema validation checks shape, not authorization.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations (Security)

stem: In Next.js 16, a Server Action calls `revalidateTag('posts')` with a single argument. What is the situation?

options.text: It is the recommended form and behaves like the `'max'` profile
options.why: The recommended form passes a profile; the one-argument form is deprecated.

options.text: Deprecated; it acts like `{ expire: 0 }`, never stale
options.why: The docs suggest `updateTag` in actions or `'max'` instead.

options.text: It throws at runtime, because a profile is now required
options.why: It still runs if TypeScript errors are suppressed, though support may be removed.

options.text: It only marks the tag; nothing happens until the next deployment
options.why: Revalidation happens on the next request, not the next deploy.

explanation: The `revalidateTag(tag)` form is deprecated in Next.js 16 and is a TypeScript error. It currently behaves like `{ expire: 0 }`, a blocking revalidation on the next request, equivalent to `updateTag`. Migrate to `updateTag` in Server Actions for read-your-own-writes, or `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')` for stale-while-revalidate.
reference: Next.js docs: revalidateTag

stem: A textarea submits its form on Ctrl+Enter. The handler calls `e.currentTarget.form?.submit()`, and the Server Action never runs. Which change makes it work like clicking the submit button?

options.text: Call `form.dispatchEvent(new Event('click'))` instead
options.why: A click event on the form element does not submit it.

options.text: Call `form.requestSubmit()` instead
options.why: It fires a real submit event, with validation, so React invokes the action.

options.text: Wrap `form.submit()` in `startTransition`
options.why: The problem is that `submit()` skips the submit event, not the scheduling.

options.text: Add `method="post"` to the form
options.why: React already dispatches the action as a POST; the attribute isn't the issue.

explanation: `HTMLFormElement.submit()` submits without firing the `submit` event and without constraint validation, so React's action handling never runs. `requestSubmit()` behaves like clicking a submit button: it validates, fires `submit`, and React invokes the Server Action on the nearest form. This is the approach the Next.js forms guide shows.
reference: Next.js docs: Forms guide (Programmatic form submission); MDN: requestSubmit

stem: A `'use server'` file `app/actions.ts` starts with `import 'server-only'`. A Client Component imports one of its actions to pass to `useActionState`. What happens at build time?

options.text: The build fails, because `server-only` forbids any import from a Client Component
options.why: The docs say this setup works.

options.text: It builds fine, because `'use server'` modules resolve in a server-only layer
options.why: The client only receives an action reference, never the module body.

options.text: It builds, but the action runs in the browser because it was imported by client code
options.why: Server Functions always run on the server.

options.text: It builds only if the import is changed to `import type`
options.why: A type-only import would remove the callable reference you need.

explanation: You can use `import 'server-only'` in both a Data Access Layer and the `'use server'` file itself. Both work when the action is imported into a Client Component, because `'use server'` modules are resolved in a server-only webpack layer. The client bundle receives only an ID plus a dispatcher.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Using a Data Access Layer for mutations)

stem: A checkout action does `throw new Error('Card declined: insufficient funds')`, and `app/checkout/error.tsx` displays `error.message`. In production, what does the user see?

options.text: The exact message, because error boundaries receive the original Error
options.why: Development forwards messages; production sanitizes server errors.

options.text: A generic message, plus an `error.digest` you can match in server logs
options.why: Production hides server error details so nothing sensitive leaks.

options.text: A 500 page from the browser, because thrown action errors skip error boundaries
options.why: Uncaught errors bubble to the nearest `error.tsx`.

options.text: Nothing: thrown errors in actions are logged and silently ignored
options.why: Thrown errors do reach an error boundary.

explanation: In production, errors forwarded from the server show a generic message with a `digest` identifier instead of the original text. Expected failures such as a declined card should be returned as values, for example `{ message: 'Card declined' }`, and rendered via `useActionState`. Reserve throwing for real bugs.
reference: Next.js docs: error.js (error.digest); Error Handling

stem: A callback scheduled with `after()` from `next/server` inside a Server Action still runs even when the action then calls `redirect()`.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: `after` runs even when the response did not complete normally, including after `redirect` or `notFound`.

options.text: False
options.why: `redirect` throwing does not cancel work already scheduled with `after`.

explanation: `after` schedules work, such as logging or analytics, to run after the response is finished. Its callbacks run even if an error is thrown or `notFound`/`redirect` is called. In Server Functions you can also read `cookies()` and `headers()` inside the callback.
reference: Next.js docs: after

stem: An action wraps its whole body in `try/catch` so it can return `{ error: 'Something went wrong' }`, but the `redirect('/done')` inside the `try` never navigates. Which fix keeps the `try/catch`?

options.text: Replace `redirect` with `permanentRedirect`, which doesn't throw
options.why: `permanentRedirect` also works by throwing, so it is caught the same way.

options.text: Call `unstable_rethrow(err)` at the top of the `catch` block
options.why: It re-throws Next.js control-flow errors and lets real errors fall through.

options.text: Return `redirect('/done')` so the value escapes the `try`
options.why: `redirect` never returns; the throw still lands in the catch.

options.text: Call `router.push('/done')` from the action instead
options.why: `useRouter` is a client hook and cannot be used in a Server Action.

explanation: `redirect` and `notFound` throw framework errors. The docs say to call `redirect` outside the `try` block, or, if you must catch broadly, use `unstable_rethrow(err)` from `next/navigation` at the start of the `catch`. That re-throws internal errors so Next.js can handle them, while your own errors are still caught.
reference: Next.js docs: unstable_rethrow; redirect (Behavior)

stem: The `/admin` page redirects non-admins in its Server Component. Its delete form calls an inline action that deletes a user without checking anything, "because only admins can see this page". Is it safe?

options.text: Yes, because the action's ID only exists in HTML sent to admins
options.why: IDs leak through browsers, logs and shared builds; they are not secrets to rely on.

options.text: Yes, because closure encryption ties the action to the admin's session
options.why: Closure encryption protects captured values; it does not authenticate callers.

options.text: No: a page-level check does not cover its actions, so re-check inside
options.why: Actions are reachable by direct POST without rendering the page.

options.text: No, but only because inline actions are disabled in production
options.why: Inline actions in Server Components are fully supported.

explanation: A page-level authentication check does not extend to the Server Actions defined within it. Render-time gating is not a security boundary, because anyone can send the same POST. Re-verify authentication and authorization inside every action, ideally in a Data Access Layer.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Authentication and authorization)

stem: Next.js encrypts Server Action IDs and periodically regenerates them. Even if your source code doesn't change, at most how many days are the IDs cached before they rotate? Type a number.
explanation: Action IDs are created during compilation and cached for at most 14 days. They are regenerated on a new build or when the build cache is invalidated. This is one reason long-lived tabs can hit "Failed to find Server Action" after a deploy.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Built-in Server Actions security features)

stem: An action parses its input with `z.object({ postId: z.string().uuid(), title: z.string().max(100) })` and the parse succeeds. Which two risks can remain? (Choose two.)

options.text: The `postId` may belong to another user, so ownership still has to be checked
options.why: Schema validation checks shape, not whether the caller may touch that row.

options.text: The caller may not be signed in at all unless the action checks the session
options.why: Validation says nothing about who sent the request.

options.text: The `title` could still be longer than 100 characters
options.why: The parse would have failed; `.max(100)` is enforced at runtime.

options.text: The `postId` might not be a valid UUID
options.why: `.uuid()` already rejects malformed IDs.

options.text: Zod output cannot be passed to the database without re-parsing it
options.why: Parsed output is safe to use as typed data.

explanation: The Next.js security guidance separates three checks: authentication (is there a session?), authorization (may this user act on this ID?) and validation (is the input well formed?). A schema handles only the last. A well-formed object can still refer to a row the caller doesn't own.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations (Security)

stem: A "Like" button calls `await like(postId)` in `onClick` with no pending state. A user double-clicks quickly, and the action increments a counter. What happens?

options.text: The second click is ignored because an action for that post is already running
options.why: Next.js queues later calls; it doesn't discard them.

options.text: Both calls run at the same time and race, so the count may go up by only 1
options.why: The client dispatches actions one at a time, so they don't overlap.

options.text: The calls run one after the other, so the count goes up by 2
options.why: The second waits for the first, then executes too.

options.text: The second call is rejected by the CSRF check as a replay
options.why: The origin check doesn't detect repeated requests.

explanation: Next.js dispatches Server Actions one at a time per client: the second waits for the first, then runs. Rapid clicks are serialized, not deduplicated. Disable the button while pending, using `useTransition` or `useActionState`, or make the mutation idempotent, for example a toggle keyed by user and post.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations (Sequential dispatch on the client)

stem: A Server Action that writes to the database but calls none of `updateTag`, `revalidatePath`, `refresh`, `cookies().set`/`.delete` or `redirect` still makes Next.js re-render the current route in its response.

options.text: True
options.why: Without one of those triggers, Next.js sends no new RSC payload.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: such an action's response carries only its return value, and the current route is not re-rendered.

explanation: The single-roundtrip UI update is opt-in. An action that does none of the listed things carries only its return value. Pages that show the mutated data stay as they are until you trigger a re-render or the user navigates.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations

stem: Which protections does Next.js apply to Server Actions by default, without any application code? (Choose three.)

options.text: Rejecting requests whose `Origin` host differs from the app's host
options.why: This is the built-in CSRF check.

options.text: Capping request bodies at 1 MB
options.why: This is the default `bodySizeLimit`.

options.text: Encrypting variables an inline action captures from its component
options.why: Closure variables are encrypted before being sent to the client.

options.text: Rate limiting each action per IP address
options.why: The docs recommend adding rate limiting yourself for expensive actions.

options.text: Requiring a signed-in session before any action runs
options.why: Authentication is the application's job inside every action.

options.text: Validating FormData against the TypeScript parameter types
options.why: Types are erased at runtime; validation needs a schema library.

explanation: Framework protections include the Origin/Host CSRF check, a 1MB body limit, encrypted non-deterministic action IDs with dead-code elimination, and closure variable encryption. Authentication, authorization, input validation, return-value shaping and rate limiting remain your responsibility.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions and Mutations (Security); Data Security

stem: A security reviewer sends a POST to a page's Server Action from a script, with the correct action ID header but no `Origin` header. How does the built-in CSRF check treat it?

options.text: It rejects the request, because a missing Origin counts as a mismatch
options.why: The docs say a request with no Origin is not rejected.

options.text: It lets the request through, with a warning
options.why: A missing Origin isn't treated as cross-site, so the action's own checks matter.

options.text: It falls back to checking the `Referer` header
options.why: The docs describe no Referer fallback.

options.text: It answers with 403 unless the IP is listed in `allowedOrigins`
options.why: Entries are hostnames for Origin matching, not client IPs.

explanation: The CSRF check compares the Origin header's host with the app's host and rejects mismatches. A request with no Origin header at all is allowed through with a warning. That is fine for blocking browser-based CSRF, but it shows why every action must still authenticate the caller itself.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions config (allowedOrigins)

stem: An app sets `serverActions.allowedOrigins: ['my-proxy.com', '*.my-proxy.com', '**.eu.my-proxy.com', 'my-proxy.com:8443']`. Match each request's Origin host with the entry that accepts it.

options.text: `my-proxy.com`
`*.my-proxy.com`
`**.eu.my-proxy.com`
`my-proxy.com:8443`
No entry; the action is rejected

explanation: Entries match the Origin host, which includes the port when there is one. `*` stands for exactly one label and `**` for one or more, and `**` is only allowed at the start. A bare host doesn't match a ported origin. Ports cannot be wildcarded, so `app.my-proxy.com:8443` needs its own `*.my-proxy.com:8443` entry.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions config (allowedOrigins)

stem: You set `bodySizeLimit: '2mb'` so users can upload images of up to exactly 2 MB through a form action. A 2,097,152-byte file still fails. Why?

options.text: Multipart boundaries and headers count toward the limit
options.why: Leave roughly 10–20 KB of headroom for multipart overhead.

options.text: `'2mb'` is parsed as 2,000,000 bytes and the file is 2 MiB
options.why: The `bytes` format uses 1,024-based units, so `'2mb'` is exactly 2,097,152 bytes.

options.text: The limit only applies after base64 encoding, which adds a third
options.why: Multipart sends file bytes as-is; nothing is base64-encoded.

options.text: Images are always rejected by actions and need a Route Handler
options.why: Actions accept files through FormData.

explanation: The limit applies to the raw HTTP request body, including the bytes `multipart/form-data` adds for boundaries, part headers and field metadata. Uploads close to the limit can exceed it, so set it a little higher, about 10–20 KB, or send large files directly to storage.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions config (bodySizeLimit)

stem: A Server Action POST arrives at a Next.js app with `allowedOrigins` configured. Put the steps of the built-in CSRF check in order.

options.text: Read the request's `Origin` header
Take the Origin's host (hostname plus port, if any)
Compare it with the app's host from `x-forwarded-host` or `host`
If they differ, look for a matching `allowedOrigins` entry
Reject the action if nothing matched; otherwise run it

explanation: Next.js compares the host in the request's Origin header with its own host, taken from `x-forwarded-host` or `host`. Only when they differ does `allowedOrigins` come into play; no match means rejection. A request without an Origin header is let through with a warning.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions config (allowedOrigins); Data Security (Allowed origins)

stem: Behind a reverse proxy, the browser shows `app.acme.io`. The proxy forwards its own host, so Next.js sees `localhost:3000`, and every action fails the CSRF check. Which fix is correct?

options.text: Add `'localhost:3000'` to `allowedOrigins`
options.why: The Origin is the public host; the internal host is what Next.js already sees.

options.text: Add `'app.acme.io'`, or forward it in `x-forwarded-host`
options.why: Either makes the Origin host acceptable.

options.text: Disable the check with `allowedOrigins: ['*']`
options.why: A lone `*` matches a single label, so it doesn't match `app.acme.io` at all.

options.text: Only add it in development, because the check is dev-only
options.why: The check runs in production as well.

explanation: When the proxy forwards the public host in `x-forwarded-host`, no entry is needed. When it sends its own host, the browser's Origin (`app.acme.io`) and the server's host (`localhost:3000`) differ, and `allowedOrigins` exists for exactly that case. Add the host in the browser's address bar, not the internal one. The check applies in production too.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions config (allowedOrigins)

stem: A sign-up form uses `useActionState`. When the email is taken, the Server Action returns `{ error: 'Email taken' }` instead of throwing. The error message appears, but the email input, rendered with `defaultValue=""`, is now empty. Why, and what keeps the user's input?

options.text: The action re-rendered the page, so remove the error return to stop it
options.why: Without the return value you lose the error message, and the reset still happens.

options.text: React resets the form after the action; echo values into `defaultValue`
options.why: A returned error still counts as a completed action, so the form resets.

options.text: The browser cleared the input because the POST response had no body
options.why: With JavaScript loaded, the submission is handled by React, not a native POST.

options.text: Next.js clears FormData after reading it; read it with `structuredClone` first
options.why: FormData is not cleared, and that wouldn't touch the DOM input.

explanation: In React 19, when a function passed to `<form action>` completes, React resets the form's uncontrolled fields. Returning `{ error }` is still a completed action, so the typed email disappears (verified with React 19.3). Return the submitted values in the state, for example `{ error, email }`, and render `defaultValue={state?.email}`, or use controlled inputs.
reference: react.dev: <form> (action reset behaviour); Next.js docs: Forms guide

stem: With the experimental `authInterrupts` flag enabled, a Server Action finds that the signed-in user may not delete a post. What does calling `forbidden()` from `next/navigation` do?

options.text: Returns `{ status: 403 }` to the caller as the action's value
options.why: It doesn't return a value; like `notFound`, it interrupts.

options.text: It interrupts, and Next.js renders `forbidden.tsx`
options.why: It is documented for Server Functions as well as Server Components and Route Handlers.

options.text: Logs a warning and lets the deletion continue
options.why: An interrupt stops the action; nothing after it runs.

options.text: Only works in Proxy, so it fails inside an action
options.why: `forbidden` is supported in Server Functions.

explanation: With `experimental.authInterrupts`, `forbidden()` and `unauthorized()` can be thrown from Server Components, Server Functions and Route Handlers. Next.js then renders the matching `forbidden.tsx` or `unauthorized.tsx` segment. Without the flag, throw an error or return a value instead. Like `redirect`, keep these calls outside a broad `try/catch` or use `unstable_rethrow`.
reference: Next.js docs: forbidden; Server Actions and Mutations (Security)
